When evaluating the performance of a locally hosted large language model, raw throughput numbers can be deceptive if not contextualized properly. The most common metric reported by inference engines such as vLLM, TGI, or Ollama is tokens per second (TPS). However, TPS is not a monolithic figure; it splits into prompt throughput and generation throughput, each reflecting a fundamentally different computational bottleneck. Prompt throughput measures how quickly the model processes the input tokens—essentially the attention mechanism’s ability to attend to the context window. Generation throughput, by contrast, measures the speed at which the model produces new tokens autoregressively, one at a time. Understanding the distinction is critical because the two phases scale differently with hardware and model size.

Prompt throughput is heavily influenced by memory bandwidth and the efficiency of the attention implementation. On a GPU, this phase is often memory-bound, meaning that the speed at which weights can be fetched from VRAM dictates performance. On a CPU, it is bound by compute and cache hierarchy. Generation throughput, however, is compute-bound and depends on the matrix multiplication capabilities of the accelerator. For large models, generation is typically the slower phase, so overall latency is dominated by generation throughput. When you see a high prompt throughput but low generation throughput, it indicates that the model is loading context quickly but struggling to generate output, often a sign of insufficient GPU compute or suboptimal quantization.

One common pitfall in benchmarking is using very short outputs to estimate generation throughput. If you ask the model to produce only a few tokens, the overhead of tokenization, kernel launches, and memory transfers becomes a significant fraction of the total time. This inflates the apparent latency per token and makes the model look slower than it truly is. For accurate generation throughput measurements, you should request outputs of at least 100–200 tokens, or better yet, measure the time to generate a fixed number of tokens across many requests and average the result. Short outputs also fail to capture the effect of KV cache growth, which can degrade performance as the context window expands.

Comparing CPU-only, GPU-only, and hybrid runs requires careful control of variables. A CPU-only run will typically show low prompt throughput and very low generation throughput, especially for models larger than 7B parameters, because CPUs lack the parallelism needed for large matrix multiplications. A GPU-only run, particularly with a modern NVIDIA card and a well-optimized inference engine, will show high prompt throughput and significantly higher generation throughput. Hybrid runs, where the model is split across CPU and GPU, can be useful when VRAM is insufficient to hold the full model. However, hybrid setups often suffer from PCIe bandwidth bottlenecks, leading to lower prompt throughput and increased latency. To compare fairly, ensure that the same model, quantization, batch size, and context length are used across all configurations. Additionally, monitor GPU utilization and memory usage; low GPU utilization in a GPU-only run may indicate that the model is too small to saturate the device, while high CPU usage in a hybrid run suggests that the offloading strategy is not optimal.

Finally, always report the hardware specifications, model size, quantization level, and batch size alongside throughput numbers. Without this context, a TPS figure is meaningless. By separating prompt and generation throughput, avoiding short-output bias, and controlling for hardware and configuration variables, you can obtain reliable, comparable measurements that reflect the true performance of your local LLM deployment.
